abstract: METR conducted a follow-up study from August 2025 to measure AI's impact on open-source developer productivity, finding initial estimates of -18% speedup for original developers and -4% for newly-recruited developers. However, the authors acknowledge severe selection biases that likely underestimate AI's true productivity effects, as developers increasingly refuse to work without AI tools and selectively avoid submitting tasks they expect AI to accelerate. The authors conclude their current experimental design produces unreliable signals and outline alternative measurement approaches.
keyFindings: Original developers from the early 2025 study now show an estimated -18% speedup with AI (confidence interval: -38% to +9%), compared to a 19% slowdown found in the February-June 2025 study.
Newly-recruited developers show an estimated -4% speedup (confidence interval: -15% to +9%), suggesting modest gains but with wide uncertainty bounds spanning zero.

Significant selection bias exists: 30-50% of developers report actively avoiding submitting tasks they expect AI to complete quickly, and recruitment/retention became harder as developers declined to participate in AI-disallowed conditions.

The authors estimate their measured productivity effects are likely lower-bound estimates due to systematic undersampling of developers with the most optimistic AI expectations and tasks with highest expected AI uplift.

Data collection challenges include variable task selection by developers using AI, differences in code quality between conditions, non-completion of AI-disallowed tasks, and difficulty measuring time spent with concurrent AI agents.
methodology: Experimental study conducted August 2025 - February 2026 with 57 developers (10 from original study, 47 newly recruited) across 143 open-source repositories and 800+ tasks. Participants were paid $50/hour to work on self-selected tasks randomized into 'AI-allowed' or 'AI-disallowed' conditions. Developers pre-specified tasks, recorded completion time, and completed surveys about selection behavior and AI use patterns. Compared results to original February-June 2025 study that found 19% slowdown (CI: +2% to +39%) among experienced open-source developers paid $150/hour.
qualifiers: The authors explicitly state the data from the new experiment 'gives us an unreliable signal of the current productivity effect' due to selection effects. They note 'weak evidence' for speedup and acknowledge 'the true speedup could be much higher among the developers and tasks which are selected out of the experiment.' Additional limitations include: lower pay rate ($50/hr vs $150/hr in original study), changes in task type selection when using AI, variable code quality between conditions, incomplete task submission in AI-disallowed conditions, and measurement challenges with agentic tools. The authors acknowledge their estimate is 'likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact.'
